slides.title: Shortest Paths and Spanning Trees
slides.main: The real world is weighted: not the fewest steps, but the smallest sum of weights.

captions: Before, every edge cost the same — BFS finds the fewest steps
Now each edge has its own weight: km, minutes, money, risk
We need the path with the smallest weight sum: S to T — Dijkstra's problem

slides.title: Dijkstra: the greedy idea
slides.main: The vertex with the smallest estimate is final: any detour would pass through a vertex with a larger estimate.

captions: Each vertex gets a distance estimate: 0 for the start, ∞ for the rest
Take the nearest vertex not yet closed: its estimate is already exact
Relaxation: is the path to a neighbor shorter through it? If so, update the estimate

slides.title: Dijkstra by hand
slides.sub: Home → Work: the direct street vs. a detour
slides.main: The direct road, picked by the first estimate, turned out worst — gradual improvement of estimates fixed the choice.

captions: All distances are infinite except the start
Close S (distance 0); relax its neighbors
Close A (distance 2); relax its neighbors
Close B (distance 3); relax its neighbors
Close C (distance 6); relax its neighbors
Close D (distance 6); relax its neighbors
Close T (distance 9); relax its neighbors

slides.title: Dijkstra with a heap
slides.main: The formula "vertices plus edges, times log of vertices" often comes up in interviews.

captions: Vertices with estimates live in a priority queue (heap)
Popped the minimum (0, S), pushed neighbor estimates
(2, A) gave (3, B) — the old (5, B) stays in the heap
A stale entry is simply skipped on pop: lazy deletion; total O((V + E) log V)

slides.title: Limit: weights are non-negative
slides.main: Before using Dijkstra, ask: does the system have discounts, refunds, negative delays?

captions: Edge B → A with weight −2
A looks closer (3 < 4), closed at 3. Via B it would be 2 — but closed vertices are not revisited
Correct answer is 2; weights must be non-negative — otherwise Bellman-Ford

slides.title: Bellman-Ford
slides.main: Improvements after V passes mean a negative cycle: there is no shortest path at all.

captions: n − 1 times, go over all edges and try to improve estimates
Pass 1 gave A = 2 and B = 4 — the negative edge is handled
If a pass changes nothing, we can stop: O(V · E)
If estimates still improve on pass n, a negative cycle is reachable

slides.title: A*: search with foresight
slides.main: Guide greed with a good estimate — it gets many times faster without breaking.

captions: Dijkstra spreads out in circles and reaches the goal after covering lots of extra ground
A* adds a "how much is left" estimate to the distance and heads for the goal
The heuristic must not overestimate the true distance — then the answer stays exact

slides.title: All pairs at once: Floyd-Warshall
slides.sub: Distance between every pair of vertices
slides.main: At large scale, all pairs are not computed — repeated Dijkstra runs do the job.

captions: Distances between all pairs: at first, direct edges only
Allow a transfer via A: D → A → B gives 2 + 3 = 5 — cell D, B updated
Transfer via B opens A → C (3 + 2 = 5) and D → C (7)
n³ time and n² memory; for small graphs — one table answers every question

slides.title: Variety of weights
slides.sub: A weight need not live on an edge
slides.main: Reducing a new problem to a known algorithm by choosing weights well is half the solution.

captions: A weight is not only km: travel time
Money, transfer penalties
Risk: multiplying probabilities becomes adding logarithms
Several criteria are folded into one weight

slides.title: Many sources at once
slides.main: Always ask yourself: is my single source really a set?

captions: Several starts: fire stations, warehouses, antennas
Put all start vertices in the queue at once — the waves run together
Every cell gets the distance to its nearest source in one pass

slides.title: Minimum spanning tree
slides.main: Cycles in a network waste cable, so the answer is always a tree.

captions: Connect everyone in the cheapest way
A spanning tree: an acyclic subgraph linking all vertices — V − 1 edges
Minimum spanning tree: smallest total weight (here 11)

slides.title: Kruskal and disjoint sets
slides.main: Kruskal is pure greed, and in chapter 10 we return to it as a proven algorithm.

captions: Sort edges by weight: A-B 1, S-A 2, C-D 2, B-D 3, D-T 3, A-C 4, …
Take the lightest ones that close no cycle
B-D joined two components into one
Five edges on six vertices — the tree is done
Edge A-C would close a cycle: disjoint sets answer in near-constant time

slides.title: Prim
slides.sub: Grow a tree from one vertex
slides.main: One idea — greedily take the best local step — serves both paths and networks.

captions: Grow a tree from one vertex
Cheapest edge outward: S-A (2)
Now A-B (1)
B-D (3) — the cheapest outgoing edge
C and T joined via edges 2 and 3: tree weight 11. A heap gives O(E log V)

slides.title: Spanning trees in the real world
slides.main: A fast skeleton makes an approximate answer possible where an exact one is intractable.

captions: Lay cable to every office at the lowest cost
Remove the k − 1 longest tree edges — get k clusters
The tree gives fast approximations for hard problems (traveling salesman)
Image segmentation by closeness of neighboring pixels

slides.main: BFS, forgetting about weights, heroically drags you through the swamp — see for yourself.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Greed works when you can prove the locally best step does not spoil the global optimum.

captions: Non-negative weights and a priority queue
Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and catches cycles
A* — a path to one goal; Floyd — all pairs
Spanning tree — the cheapest link of all vertices
